title: 22. Interview: Redis
summary: Interview Q&A for Redis — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Redis interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Why is Redis single-threaded, and how does it still achieve 100k+ ops/sec?
**Answer:** Redis uses a single-threaded event loop with `epoll`/`kqueue` for non-blocking I/O. The main loop calls `epoll_wait` to get ready file descriptors, processes each command sequentially, and writes responses — all without spawning threads or taking locks. This is fast because: **(1) No lock contention** — every operation is atomic by definition, no time spent acquiring/releasing mutexes. **(2) No context switching** — the CPU stays in the Redis process, caches stay hot. **(3) Memory is the bottleneck, not CPU** — at memory bandwidth, a single thread can do 100k+ ops/sec on commodity hardware; adding threads doesn't make RAM faster. **(4) Most commands are O(1) or O(log N)** — `SET`, `GET`, `INCR`, `HSET`, `ZADD` are all sub-microsecond. The trade-off: a single Redis process can't use multiple CPU cores (you run one process per core, sharding across them via Redis Cluster). Long-running commands block the event loop — `KEYS *` on a million-key database blocks for seconds, freezing all clients. Redis provides `SCAN` (cursor-based, returns partial results) instead, and `DEBUG SLEEP` is disabled in production. Newer Redis versions (6.0+) added I/O threading for network reads/writes (still single-threaded command execution), which doubles throughput on high-network-bandwidth scenarios. Real-world: Stack Overflow's Redis instance handles 100k+ ops/sec on a single core for caching.
**Visual:**
```
Single-threaded event loop:

  +------+ +------+ +------+
  | C1   | | C2   | | C3   |  (clients)
  +--+---+ +--+---+ +--+---+
     |        |        |
     v        v        v
  +--+--------+--------+----+
  | epoll_wait (ready FDs)  |
  +-----------+------------+
              |
              v
  +-----------+------------+
  | while True:            |
  |   events = epoll_wait()|
  |   for fd in events:    |
  |     cmd = read(fd)     |
  |     res = exec(cmd)    |  <-- atomic, no locks
  |     write(fd, res)     |
  +------------------------+
              |
              v
  +------------------------+
  | In-memory hash table   |
  | (strings, lists, ...)  |
  +------------------------+

Why fast:
  + No lock contention (atomic by design)
  + No context switching (one thread)
  + Memory-bound, not CPU-bound
  + Most commands O(1) or O(log N)

Why 100k+ ops/sec on one core:
  - L1/L2 cache hit on hot keys
  - No syscall per op (epoll batches)
  - Redis protocol (RESP) is simple to parse
```

### Q2. What's the difference between RDB and AOF persistence, and which should you use?
**Answer:** **RDB (Redis Database)** snapshots the entire dataset to disk periodically (e.g., `save 900 1` means save if >=1 key changed in 15 min). It uses `fork()` — the child process writes the snapshot while the parent keeps serving traffic (copy-on-write memory means the parent doesn't block). RDB is compact (binary), fast to load on restart, and good for backups. The trade-off: data loss between snapshots (potentially minutes of writes). **AOF (Append-Only File)** logs every write command to a file as it happens. The `fsync` policy controls durability: `always` (fsync every write, slowest, zero data loss), `everysec` (fsync once per second, default, at most 1 second of data loss), `no` (let OS handle it, fastest, potentially large loss on crash). AOF replay on restart re-executes every command — slow for large files, but Redis 4.0+ does **AOF rewrite** (compacts the log by computing current state). The recommended production setup is **both RDB + AOF**: RDB for fast restart and backups (copy the RDB file offsite nightly), AOF for durability (at most 1 second of data loss). If you can tolerate minutes of data loss (pure cache), RDB alone is fine. If you can't tolerate any loss (session store), AOF `always` is required but slow. Real-world: Stack Overflow uses AOF `everysec` for their caching layer (1 second of loss is OK); a financial app uses AOF `always` for the rate-limiter state (any loss could double-process a payment).
**Visual:**
```
                    RDB                    AOF
                    ---                    ---
Mechanism         Periodic snapshot       Append every write
                  (fork + save)           to log file
fsync policy      N/A (snapshot)          always / everysec / no
Data loss         minutes (since last     0 / 1s / unbounded
                  snapshot)
Restart speed     fast (load binary)      slow (replay commands)
File size         small (binary)          large (until rewrite)
Backups           easy (copy RDB file)    harder (large, growing)
Rewrite           N/A                     yes (compact log)
CPU on write      fork (COW, minimal)     append (minimal)
Disk I/O pattern  bursty (snapshot)       continuous (per write)

When to use:
  Pure cache (rebuildable)        -> RDB only (or none)
  Session store (1s loss OK)      -> AOF everysec
  Critical state (0 loss)         -> AOF always (slow)
  Production general-purpose      -> BOTH RDB + AOF everysec
                                     (RDB for backups, AOF for durability)

Redis 4.0+ "mixed" AOF rewrite:
  rewrite produces RDB-format snapshot + AOF-format incremental
  -> fast restart (load RDB) + durable (replay AOF tail)
```

### Q3. How does Redis Cluster shard data, and what's the role of hash tags?
**Answer:** Redis Cluster divides the key space into **16,384 hash slots**. Each key is hashed with `CRC16(key) mod 16384` to get a slot number. Each slot is owned by exactly one master node (with a replica for failover). A 3-master cluster has ~5461 slots per master. Clients can connect to any node; if the node doesn't own the slot for the requested key, it returns a `MOVED <slot> <ip:port>` redirect. Smart clients (redis-py, ioredis, Jedis) cache the slot map and route directly to the owning node after the first redirect, avoiding overhead. **Hash tags** force multiple keys to the same slot — if a key contains `{...}`, only the substring inside `{}` is hashed. So `{user:42}:profile` and `{user:42}:settings` both hash to the slot for `user:42`, landing on the same master. This enables multi-key operations like `MGET {user:42}:profile {user:42}:settings` or `MULTI/EXEC` transactions across multiple keys, which would otherwise fail with `CROSSSLOT` errors. Real-world: a social app uses `{user:alice}:profile`, `{user:alice}:followers`, `{user:alice}:timeline` so all of Alice's data lives on one shard, enabling atomic operations on her profile + followers. The trade-off: hash tags can cause hot shards if one user (e.g., a celebrity) generates disproportionate traffic — you need to monitor slot distribution and rebalance if needed.
**Visual:**
```
Redis Cluster (3 masters, 3 replicas):

  Slot   0-5460     -> M1 (R1)
  Slot 5461-10922   -> M2 (R2)
  Slot 10923-16383  -> M3 (R3)

  Client sends: GET user:42
    CRC16("user:42") mod 16384 = 12345
    -> slot 12345 owned by M3
    -> client sends to M3, gets value

  Client (dumb) sends to M1 by mistake:
    M1 returns: -MOVED 12345 10.0.0.3:6379
    Client retries on M3, caches slot map

  Multi-key problem:
    MGET user:42:profile user:42:settings
    -> CRC16 differs -> CROSSSLOT error!

  Solution: hash tags
    MGET {user:42}:profile {user:42}:settings
    -> only "user:42" is hashed -> same slot -> works!

  Real-world key design:
    {user:alice}:profile    -> hash slot of "user:alice"
    {user:alice}:followers  -> same slot
    {user:alice}:timeline   -> same slot
    {user:alice}:settings   -> same slot
    -> all of Alice's data on one shard
    -> atomic MULTI/EXEC across her keys
    -> trade-off: hot user = hot shard (monitor!)

  Rebalancing:
    redis-cli --cluster reshard <node>:6379
      --cluster-from <src-node-id>
      --cluster-to <dst-node-id>
      --cluster-slots 1000
    -> moves 1000 slots from src to dst
    -> MIGRATE command streams keys online
```

### Q4. What is a Redis sorted set (zset), and why is it perfect for leaderboards?
**Answer:** A **sorted set (zset)** is a Redis data structure where each member has a numeric score, and members are kept sorted by score. Internally, Redis uses a **skiplist + hash table** combo: the hash table gives O(1) member lookup, the skiplist gives O(log N) range queries. Key operations: `ZADD key score member` (insert or update), `ZRANGE key start stop` (range by rank), `ZRANGEBYSCORE key min max` (range by score), `ZREVRANGE key 0 9` (top 10 descending), `ZINCRBY key delta member` (increment score atomically), `ZREMRANGEBYRANK` (trim to top N). For leaderboards: when a player's score changes, `ZINCRBY leaderboard:global 100 player_42` atomically updates their score. To display the top 10: `ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global 0 9 WITHSCORES` returns in O(log N + 10) — sub-millisecond even for millions of members. To find a player's rank: `ZREVRANK leaderboard:global player_42`. To get the player's neighbors: `ZREVRANGE leaderboard:global (rank-5) (rank+5)`. All these are O(log N) — they scale gracefully. Real-world: Reddit's "karma" leaderboard, Stack Overflow's reputation rankings, and gaming leaderboards (League of Legends, Clash Royale) all use Redis zsets. Twitter uses zsets for timelines: each user's timeline is a zset keyed by `user_id`, with `post_id` as member and `timestamp` as score — `ZREVRANGE timeline:alice 0 49` returns the latest 50 posts in sub-millisecond.
**Visual:**
```
ZSET internal structure (skiplist + hash):

  zset: leaderboard:global
  +------------------------+
  | Hash table             |     Skiplist (sorted by score)
  | member -> score        |     (multi-level linked list)
  | -------------------    |     L3: 100 -----------------> 500
  | alice -> 100           |     L2: 100 -----> 300 -----> 500
  | bob   -> 300           |     L1: 100 -> 200 -> 300 -> 400 -> 500
  | carol -> 500           |          |      |      |      |      |
  | dave  -> 400           |          v      v      v      v      v
  | eve   -> 200           |        alice   eve    bob   dave  carol
  +------------------------+

  Operations (all O(log N)):
    ZADD lb 100 alice              -> insert alice with score 100
    ZINCRBY lb 50 alice            -> alice score -> 150 (atomic)
    ZREVRANGE lb 0 9 WITHSCORES    -> top 10 (desc by score)
    ZREVRANK lb alice              -> alice's rank (0-based)
    ZRANGEBYSCORE lb 100 200       -> members with score in [100,200]
    ZREMRANGEBYRANK lb 0 -1001     -> keep top 1000 (trim)

  Use cases:
    + Gaming leaderboards (millions of players)
    + Twitter timelines (post_id, score=timestamp)
    + Reddit hot page (score = upvotes - downvotes + time decay)
    + Real-time analytics ("top URLs in last hour")
    + Priority queues (score = priority, ZPOPMIN pops highest priority)

  Why perfect for leaderboards:
    + Atomic ZINCRBY (concurrent updates safe)
    + O(log N) rank/range queries (fast at any scale)
    + Sorted in real-time (no re-indexing needed)
    + Single Redis command for top-N (no app-side sort)
```

### Q5. What's the difference between Redis Pub/Sub and Redis Streams?
**Answer:** **Pub/Sub** is fire-and-forget: publishers `PUBLISH channel message`, subscribers `SUBSCRIBE channel`, Redis routes messages to all current subscribers instantly. If no subscriber is listening, the message is dropped; if a subscriber disconnects and reconnects, it misses messages sent during the disconnect. Pub/Sub is perfect for **real-time fan-out where durability doesn't matter** — chat, live notifications, websocket push, "user just logged in" events. **Streams** (Redis 5.0+) are durable append-only logs: producers `XADD stream * field1 v1 field2 v2` append messages with auto-generated IDs (timestamp-based); messages persist until explicitly trimmed (`XTRIM` or `XADD ... MAXLEN ~1000`); consumers read with `XREAD` (any consumer sees all messages) or join a **consumer group** (`XGROUP CREATE`, `XREADGROUP`) where each message is delivered to exactly one consumer in the group. Consumers ack with `XACK`; unacked messages can be claimed by other consumers via `XCLAIM` (for crash recovery). Streams support **backlog reading** — a consumer that was offline can read from any past ID. Real-world: a chat app uses Pub/Sub for typing indicators (ephemeral, broadcast) and Streams for message delivery (durable, exactly-once per consumer group). The trade-off: Streams have more overhead than Pub/Sub (persistence, ack tracking), so for ephemeral broadcasts Pub/Sub is faster. Many companies replaced Kafka with Redis Streams for medium-throughput queues (100k msgs/sec) where Kafka's ops overhead isn't justified.
**Visual:**
```
Pub/Sub (fire-and-forget):

  Publisher -> PUBLISH chat "hello"
                   |
                   v
              +---------+
              | Redis   |  routes to all current subscribers
              +---------+
              /    |    \
             v     v     v
          Sub1   Sub2   Sub3

  Sub4 connects AFTER publish -> MISSES the message.
  Sub2 disconnects briefly -> MISSES messages during gap.
  No persistence, no replay, no ack.

  Use: typing indicators, presence, ephemeral broadcasts.

Streams (durable log):

  Producer -> XADD messages * text "hello"
                   |
                   v
              +---------+
              | Stream  |  (append-only log, persists)
              | ------- |
              | 1-0 hello|
              | 1-1 world|  <- messages stay until XTRIM
              | 1-2 foo  |
              +---------+
              /    |    \
             v     v     v
          C1     C2     C3   (consumer group "workers")
          reads  reads  reads
          1-0    1-1    1-2
          acks   acks   (crashes, no ack)

  C4 joins group later -> can read PEL (pending entries list)
                          of crashed C3 via XCLAIM
  C5 reads stream directly (XREAD) -> sees ALL messages
                                       (not in any group)

  Use: durable queues, event sourcing, exactly-once delivery.
```

### Q6. How do you implement a distributed lock with Redis, and what are the pitfalls?
**Answer:** The naive pattern: `SET lock_key <random_value> NX PX 30000` (set if not exists, with 30s expiry). The `NX` flag makes it atomic (no race between `GET` and `SET`); the random value identifies the lock owner. To release: check the value matches (so you don't release someone else's lock), then `DEL`. This check-and-del must be atomic — use a Lua script: `if redis.call("get", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call("del", KEYS[1]) else return 0 end`. **Pitfalls**: **(1) Lock expiry while holder is still working** — if the holder pauses (GC, network delay) longer than the TTL, the lock expires and another client acquires it; both think they hold the lock. The TTL must be longer than the worst-case operation time, with safety margin. **(2) Single-instance failure** — if the Redis instance holding the lock dies, the lock is lost. Use **Redlock** (multiple Redis instances, acquire on majority) for higher availability — though Redlock is controversial (Martin Kleppmann argued it has correctness edge cases under GC pauses). **(3) Clock drift** — if Redis servers' clocks differ, TTL calculations can be wrong. **(4) Fencing tokens** — even with a perfect lock, the protected resource (e.g., a database) needs its own monotonic fencing token to reject stale operations. Real-world: many production systems use Redis locks successfully for low-stakes coordination (cache invalidation, job deduplication) but use ZooKeeper or etcd for high-stakes coordination (leader election, distributed transactions) because those systems provide stronger guarantees (linearizability, fencing tokens built-in).
**Visual:**
```
Naive Redis lock:

  Client A: SET lock "A_nonce" NX PX 30000   -> OK (acquired)
  Client A: <does work, takes 35s due to GC pause>
  T=30s:    lock expires automatically
  T=31s:    Client B: SET lock "B_nonce" NX PX 30000  -> OK (acquired)
            (B thinks it has exclusive access)
  T=35s:    Client A: finishes, releases lock
            Lua: if get(lock) == "A_nonce" then del(lock)
                 -> value is "B_nonce", NOT deleted (good!)
            BUT A may have written to the protected resource
            already, thinking it held the lock.

  Mitigation: TTL > worst-case operation time + safety margin.

Redlock (5 Redis instances):

  Client A: SET lock on R1, R2, R3, R4, R5 (in parallel)
            -> acquired on R1, R2, R3 (majority)
            -> records time-to-acquire, computes remaining TTL
  Client B: tries same -> fails on majority (A has it)
  Release:  DEL on all 5 instances

  Pros: survives 2 of 5 instance failures
  Cons: doesn't survive long GC pauses (still subject to pitfall #1)
        Martin Kleppmann: not truly safe under GC / clock drift

  Use for: low-stakes (cache invalidation, job dedup)
  Use ZooKeeper/etcd for: high-stakes (leader election,
                           distributed transactions)
                           (they provide fencing tokens)
```

### Q7. What is the difference between Redis's MULTI/EXEC transactions and Lua scripts?
**Answer:** Both provide atomicity, but with different semantics. **MULTI/EXEC** queues commands on the client, then sends them as a batch to Redis, which executes them sequentially without interruption. Other clients can't interleave commands between `MULTI` and `EXEC`. **WATCH key1 key2** before `MULTI` provides **optimistic locking** — if any watched key changes before `EXEC`, the entire transaction is aborted (returns nil). Limitations: **(1) No conditional logic** — you can't say "if key1 > 5 then INCR key2 else SET key3". **(2) No loops or computed values** — you must precompute on the client. **(3) WATCH can fail under contention** — high retry rates. **Lua scripts** are server-side programs executed atomically: `EVAL "..." numkeys key1 key2 arg1 arg2`. The script can read keys, conditionally update, loop, compute — all atomically (no other command interleaves). Lua is the killer feature for complex atomic operations: rate limiters ("if count < limit then incr count else return error"), atomic swaps, conditional updates, leaderboards with custom scoring. **Performance**: Lua scripts run on the server (no round trips for intermediate reads), so a 5-command Lua script is one network round trip vs. 5 for MULTI/EXEC. **Caveat**: long-running Lua scripts block the event loop (single-threaded!), so they must be fast (sub-millisecond). Redis has `lua-time-limit` (default 5 seconds) — scripts exceeding it can be killed with `SCRIPT KILL`. Real-world: Discord uses Lua scripts for atomic presence updates; rate-limiting libraries (e.g., redis-cell) are implemented as Lua.
**Visual:**
```
MULTI/EXEC transaction (client-side queue):

  Client: WATCH counter
          MULTI
          INCR counter
          SET last_updated <ts>
          EXEC

  -> server queues [INCR counter, SET last_updated ...]
  -> executes atomically, no other client interleaves
  -> if counter changed between WATCH and EXEC -> returns nil

  Limitations:
    - no conditional logic (can't "if counter > 5 then...")
    - no loops, no computed values (client must precompute)
    - WATCH can fail under contention (retry storms)

Lua script (server-side, atomic):

  Client: EVAL "
    local c = redis.call('GET', KEYS[1])
    if tonumber(c) < tonumber(ARGV[1]) then
      redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
      redis.call('SET', KEYS[2], ARGV[2])
      return 1
    else
      return 0
    end
  " 2 counter last_updated 5 "2024-01-01"

  -> entire script runs atomically
  -> conditional logic, loops, computed values OK
  -> 1 network round trip (vs 2+ for MULTI/EXEC)
  - must be fast (blocks event loop)
  - lua-time-limit = 5s (SCRIPT KILL aborts)

Use:
  MULTI/EXEC -> simple sequential atomic updates
  Lua        -> conditional, computed, multi-step atomic ops
                (rate limiters, atomic swaps, custom leaderboards)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. You're building a Twitter-style timeline that must return a user's latest 50 posts in <5ms. How do you use Redis?
**Answer:** Use a **sorted set per user** keyed by `timeline:<user_id>`, with `post_id` as the member and `timestamp` as the score. When a user posts, fan out: for each follower, `ZADD timeline:<follower_id> <timestamp> <post_id>`. To read: `ZREVRANGE timeline:<user_id> 0 49` (descending by score = newest first). This is O(log N + 50) — sub-millisecond even for users with millions of posts in their timeline. **TTL**: set a TTL of 7 days on each timeline key so old data expires (use `EXPIRE timeline:<user_id> 604800` after each ZADD). **Trim**: `ZREMRANGEBYRANK timeline:<user_id> 0 -1001` keeps only the latest 1000 posts (avoids unbounded growth). **Celebrity problem**: a user with 10M followers would trigger 10M ZADDs per post — too slow. Use **hybrid fan-out**: for normal users (<10k followers), fan out on write; for celebrities, don't fan out — instead, when a follower reads their timeline, merge their precomputed timeline with the celebrity's latest posts (stored in a separate `posts:<celebrity_id>` zset). **Cache miss**: if a user's timeline isn't in Redis (evicted), fall back to a database query and repopulate. **Sharding**: use Redis Cluster with hash tags `{user:alice}:timeline`, `{user:alice}:profile` so all of Alice's data is on one shard. Real-world: Twitter's actual timeline is more sophisticated (they use a mix of Redis, Manhattan, and custom services), but the Redis zset pattern is the foundation.
**Visual:**
```
Timeline storage:

  ZSET timeline:alice
    member: post_id, score: timestamp
    -> (post_3, 1700000500), (post_1, 1700000300), (post_2, 1700000100)

  Read latest 50:
    ZREVRANGE timeline:alice 0 49 WITHSCORES
    -> O(log N + 50), sub-millisecond

Write fan-out (Alice posts, 1000 followers):
  for follower in alice.followers:
    ZADD timeline:<follower> <ts> <post_id>
    EXPIRE timeline:<follower> 604800  (7-day TTL)
    ZREMRANGEBYRANK timeline:<follower> 0 -1001  (keep last 1000)

Celebrity fan-out (Kim K, 10M followers):
  DO NOT fan out.
  XADD posts:kim_k * post_id <id> ts <ts>  (or ZADD)
  (followers merge kim_k's latest on read)

  Read for follower Bob (follows Alice + Kim K):
    1. ZREVRANGE timeline:bob 0 49
    2. ZREVRANGE posts:kim_k 0 49 (last hour)
    3. merge + sort by ts, return top 50

Cluster sharding:
  {user:alice}:timeline -> all on one shard (hash tag)
  {user:alice}:profile  -> same shard
  -> atomic operations across Alice's keys
```

### Q2. Your Redis-backed rate limiter needs to handle 100k requests/sec per user. The naive `INCR + EXPIRE` approach has race conditions. How do you fix it?
**Answer:** The naive pattern `INCR counter; if counter == 1 then EXPIRE counter 60` has a race: if the process crashes between `INCR` and `EXPIRE`, the counter never expires, blocking the user forever. The correct pattern uses **Lua scripting** for atomic check-and-set: `local c = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1]); if c == 1 then redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1]) end; return c`. The entire script runs atomically — no race. For 100k req/sec per user, this single-key approach creates a **hot key** (all 100k ops hit one Redis instance per second), which doesn't shard and bottlenecks the single-threaded event loop. Solutions: **(1) Sliding window with multiple buckets**: store per-second counters in a hash (`HSET rl:user:42 1700000001 1 1700000002 1 ...`), sum the last 60 seconds on read, trim old buckets. This distributes load but is more complex. **(2) Token bucket with periodic refill**: maintain `tokens` and `last_refill` per user, refill on read using elapsed time. Atomic via Lua. (3) **Approximate counting**: use multiple sub-counters per user (e.g., 10 shards), increment a random shard, sum on read. Trades 1% accuracy for 10× throughput. Real-world: Cloudflare uses sliding-window counters with Redis for their rate limiter; Stripe uses token buckets; many CDNs use approximate counting (HyperLogLog-like) at the edge. The right choice depends on accuracy needs vs. throughput.
**Visual:**
```
Naive (race condition):

  INCR counter          -> counter = 1
  <process crashes>     -> EXPIRE never runs
                          -> counter stays at 1 forever
                          -> user locked out

Fix with Lua (atomic):

  EVAL "
    local c = redis.call('INCR', KEYS[1])
    if c == 1 then
      redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[1])
    end
    return c
  " 1 rl:user:42 60

  -> entire script runs atomically, no race
  -> BUT: 100k ops/sec on one key = hot key
     (single Redis instance bottlenecked)

Hot-key solutions:

  Option A: sliding window with hash buckets
    HSET rl:user:42 <unix_second> 1   (per-second bucket)
    HINCRBY rl:user:42 <unix_second> 1
    read: sum last 60 buckets
    trim: HDEL old buckets
    -> distributes load across 60 keys

  Option B: token bucket (Lua):
    local t = redis.call('TIME')
    local elapsed = t - last_refill
    local tokens = min(capacity, tokens + elapsed * rate)
    if tokens >= 1 then
      tokens = tokens - 1
      last_refill = t
      return 1  (allowed)
    else
      return 0  (blocked)
    end

  Option C: sharded counters (approximate)
    shard = random(0..9)
    INCR rl:user:42:shard<shard>
    read: SUM all 10 shards (10 ops, parallelizable)
    -> 10x throughput, ~1% accuracy loss
```

### Q3. Your Redis cache has a 95% hit rate, but during traffic spikes the hit rate drops to 70% and the database gets crushed. What's happening and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** This is the classic **cache stampede** (or "dog-pile") problem. When popular keys expire simultaneously (or get evicted during a spike), hundreds of requests miss the cache and hit the database simultaneously — the database gets crushed, response times spike, more requests pile up, cascading failure. Three fixes: **(1) Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch)** — when reading a cached value, with a small probability (based on remaining TTL), refresh the cache in the background while still serving the slightly-stale value to other readers. This spreads refreshes over time, avoiding the thundering herd. Implementation: store `(value, computed_at, ttl)` in Redis; on read, if `now - computed_at > ttl - random_jitter`, refresh in background. **(2) Locking on cache miss** — when a cache miss occurs, acquire a Redis lock (`SET lock:<key> NX PX 5000`); only the lock holder queries the database and writes the cache; other readers wait briefly and retry the cache read. This ensures only one database query per key per refresh window. **(3) Stale-while-revalidate** — set two TTLs: the "fresh" TTL (e.g., 5 min) and the "stale" TTL (e.g., 10 min). Reads after the fresh TTL return stale data and trigger a background refresh; reads after the stale TTL block until refresh completes. Real-world: Facebook uses probabilistic early expiration; Netflix uses locking on cache miss for their recommendation service; Stripe uses stale-while-revalidate for merchant config.
**Visual:**
```
Cache stampede:

  T=0   key X cached, TTL=5min
  T=4:59 1000 requests/sec all HIT cache (good)
  T=5:00 key X expires
  T=5:00 1000 requests all MISS cache -> all hit database
  T=5:01 database: 1000 concurrent queries -> CPU 100%, slow
  T=5:02 more requests pile up -> cascading failure

Fix #1: probabilistic early refresh (XFetch)

  On read of cached value (with computed_at, ttl):
    remaining = ttl - (now - computed_at)
    if remaining < threshold:
      p = 1 - remaining/threshold   (probability rises as TTL nears)
      if random() < p:
        refresh in background (don't block current read)
    return cached value (possibly slightly stale)

  -> refreshes spread out over threshold window (e.g., 30s)
  -> no thundering herd at expiry

Fix #2: lock on miss

  On cache miss:
    if SET lock:<key> NX PX 5000 (acquired):
      value = db.query(<key>)   (only ONE query)
      cache.set(<key>, value)
      DEL lock:<key>
    else:
      sleep(50ms)
      retry cache.get(<key>)   (other readers wait)

Fix #3: stale-while-revalidate

  cached value has:
    fresh_ttl = 5 min (return as fresh)
    stale_ttl = 10 min (return as stale, trigger background refresh)
    expired   = after 10 min (block until refresh)

  T=0:00  cached, fresh
  T=4:00  read -> fresh (good)
  T=5:30  read -> stale, async refresh, return stale value
  T=6:00  read -> fresh again (background refresh completed)
  T=10:00 read -> expired, block until refresh (rare)

Best: combine #1 (XFetch) for normal case + #2 (lock) as safety net
```

### Q4. You need to use Redis as a message queue for order processing. Should you use Lists, Streams, or Pub/Sub?
**Answer:** Use **Streams** for durable order processing. Here's why each falls short: **Pub/Sub** is fire-and-forget — if a consumer is offline when an order is published, the order is lost. Unacceptable for orders. **Lists** (`LPUSH` to enqueue, `BRPOP` to dequeue) are durable and simple, but they lack: (a) consumer groups (one consumer per queue; can't parallelize across workers safely — `RPOPLPUSH` to a "processing" list is a hack); (b) ack tracking (if a worker crashes after `RPOP` but before processing, the order is lost); (c) replay (can't re-read past orders). **Streams** solve all of these: `XADD orders * order_id 42 amount 100` enqueues durably; `XGROUP CREATE orders workers $` creates a consumer group; `XREADGROUP GROUP workers consumer-1 COUNT 1 STREAMS orders >` delivers one order to one consumer; `XACK orders workers <message_id>` confirms processing. If a consumer crashes, its pending messages (PEL) can be claimed by another consumer via `XAUTOCLAIM`. Streams also support `XTRIM` to bound the backlog (e.g., `MAXLEN ~ 1000000` keeps last million orders). The trade-off vs. Kafka: Redis Streams are simpler to operate (no ZooKeeper, no separate broker) but max out around 100k msgs/sec per shard; Kafka handles millions of msgs/sec. For order processing (typically <10k orders/sec per service), Redis Streams is the right choice. Real-world: many e-commerce platforms use Redis Streams for order processing; the durability + consumer group semantics match the use case perfectly. Use Lists only for trivial ephemeral queues; use Pub/Sub only for ephemeral broadcasts.
**Visual:**
```
Queue options comparison:

  Pub/Sub:
    XADD orders * ... no, XADD is stream
    PUBLISH orders <payload>
    -> subscribers receive instantly
    -> if no subscriber, DROPPED (lost order!)
    -> no ack, no replay
    Verdict: NEVER for orders.

  Lists:
    LPUSH orders <payload>
    BRPOP orders <timeout>
    -> durable (persists in list)
    -> but: only one consumer can RPOP at a time
    -> if consumer crashes after RPOP, message LOST
    -> hack: RPOPLPUSH to "processing" list, then LREM
       (complex, error-prone)
    -> no consumer groups, no ack tracking
    Verdict: too primitive for orders.

  Streams:
    XADD orders * order_id 42 amount 100
    XGROUP CREATE orders workers $    (create group at end)
    XREADGROUP GROUP workers c1 COUNT 1 STREAMS orders >
      -> delivers to c1, added to PEL (pending entries list)
    process order...
    XACK orders workers <msg_id>
      -> removes from PEL

    if c1 crashes:
      XAUTOCLAIM orders workers c2 <min-idle-ms> 0
        -> c2 takes over c1's pending messages
        -> at-least-once delivery

    XTRIM orders MAXLEN ~ 1000000  (bound backlog)

  Verdict: Streams are right for orders.
  Trade-off: max ~100k msgs/sec/shard (Kafka for more).
```

### Q5. Your team uses Redis for session storage. After a Redis failover, ~1% of users get logged out. Why, and how do you prevent it?
**Answer:** Two causes: **(1) Asynchronous replication lag** — Redis Cluster uses async replication from master to replica. If the master dies right after a session write but before replicating to the replica, that session is lost — the user's next request hits the new primary (old replica), doesn't find the session, and logs them out. With `everysec` AOF and async replication, the data-loss window is up to 1 second of writes — at 1000 session writes/sec, that's ~1000 lost sessions per failover (1% of 100k users). **(2) Client-side connection caching** — some clients cache the slot map; after failover, they may briefly route to the dead master, get errors, and log users out. Fixes: **(a) Use `WAIT` command** — `SET session:abc <data> ; WAIT 1 100` waits for at least 1 replica to ack the write before returning (100ms timeout). This reduces the data-loss window at the cost of ~10ms latency per write. For session storage, this trade-off is usually worth it. **(b) Use Redis sentinel** instead of cluster for single-instance HA (simpler, but no sharding). **(c) Accept the loss** — for many apps, 1% of users getting logged out per failover (which happens rarely) is acceptable. Add a "remember me" cookie that re-establishes the session transparently. **(d) Multi-AZ deployment** — run Redis across AZs so a single-AZ failure doesn't trigger failover. **(e) Session rehydration** — store a long-lived refresh token in a cookie; on session miss, validate the refresh token and re-create the session. Real-world: Netflix uses `WAIT 1` for critical session writes; GitHub uses multi-AZ Redis with cross-AZ replication; many apps just accept the 1% loss.
**Visual:**
```
Failover data loss:

  T=0  Master M1, Replica R1 (async)
  T=1  Client: SET session:abc "user_data"  -> M1 acks immediately
  T=1  M1 starts replicating to R1 (in flight, NOT yet applied)
  T=1.001 M1 crashes (power loss)
  T=2  Sentinel detects M1 down (~10s)
  T=12 R1 promoted to master
  T=13 Client: GET session:abc -> nil (R1 never got the write)
  T=14 User logged out

  Probability: depends on write rate and replication lag.
  1000 writes/sec, 1ms lag -> 1 write lost per failover (low)
  1000 writes/sec, 100ms lag -> 100 writes lost per failover

Fixes:

  (a) WAIT command (synchronous replication, optional):
      SET session:abc "user_data"
      WAIT 1 100   -> wait for 1 replica to ack (100ms timeout)
      -> trade-off: +10ms latency per session write
      -> use for critical session writes only

  (b) Multi-AZ Redis with cross-AZ replication:
      M1 in AZ-a, R1 in AZ-b, R2 in AZ-c
      + WAIT 2 (require both replicas)
      -> survives single-AZ failure with no data loss

  (c) Accept loss + transparent re-login:
      Long-lived refresh token in cookie.
      On session miss:
        if refresh_token valid:
          recreate session (transparent to user)
        else:
          redirect to login
      -> user doesn't notice the 1% loss

  (d) Don't use Redis for sessions if 0% loss is required:
      Use a strongly-consistent store (PostgreSQL, DynamoDB
      with strong consistency). Slower but durable.

Best practice: (c) + multi-AZ + WAIT 1 for new sessions.
```

### Q6. You're caching database query results in Redis. Some queries are slow (2s), and you want to ensure they don't run more than once every 5 minutes. How?
**Answer:** Use the **cache-aside pattern with probabilistic early refresh (XFetch) and a per-key lock** to prevent multiple concurrent refreshes. The pattern: **(1) Read path**: `GET cache:<query_hash>`. If hit, return the cached value (computing "is this stale?" via XFetch logic — if within the refresh window, kick off a background refresh). If miss, acquire a Redis lock (`SET lock:<query_hash> <nonce> NX PX 10000`); if you get the lock, run the slow query, write the result with TTL=5min, release the lock; if you don't get the lock, wait briefly and retry the cache read (another worker is refreshing). **(2) Write path**: after writing to the database, explicitly `DEL cache:<query_hash>` to invalidate (so the next read picks up fresh data). **(3) XFetch logic**: store `(value, computed_at, ttl=300s)` as a JSON object; on read, compute `remaining = ttl - (now - computed_at)`; if `remaining < 60s` (refresh window), with probability `1 - remaining/60`, kick off a background refresh; return the cached value to the current reader (slightly stale but fast). This ensures: the slow query never runs more than once per refresh window (lock); popular keys are refreshed before they expire (XFetch); cache misses don't crush the database (lock + retry). Real-world: Facebook's memcached layer uses this pattern; GitHub uses it for repository metadata caching. The query hash ensures identical SQL strings share a cache entry; consider normalizing whitespace and parameterizing.
**Visual:**
```
Cache-aside with XFetch + lock:

  Read path:
    cached = GET cache:<query_hash>
    if cached:
      value, computed_at, ttl = parse(cached)
      remaining = ttl - (now - computed_at)
      if remaining < 60:  # refresh window
        p = 1 - remaining/60
        if random() < p:
          spawn_background(refresh, query_hash)  # async, non-blocking
      return value  # may be slightly stale

    else:  # cache miss
      if SET lock:<query_hash> <nonce> NX PX 10000:  # got lock
        value = run_slow_query()  # 2s
        SET cache:<query_hash> <value, now, 300> EX 300
        DEL lock:<query_hash>
        return value
      else:  # another worker refreshing
        sleep(100ms)
        return read_path(query_hash)  # retry

  Write path (after DB write):
    DEL cache:<query_hash>  # invalidate

  XFetch effect:
    T=0:00  cached, fresh (remaining=300s)
    T=4:00  read -> fresh, no refresh
    T=4:30  read -> remaining=30, p=0.5, maybe refresh (background)
    T=4:50  read -> remaining=10, p=0.83, very likely refresh
    T=5:00  read -> if not yet refreshed, would be expired (rare)

  Benefits:
    + slow query runs at most once per 5min window (lock)
    + popular keys proactively refreshed before expiry (XFetch)
    + cache miss doesn't crush DB (lock + retry)
    + write invalidates immediately (no stale reads after write)
```

### Q7. You have 1TB of data in Redis. Memory is expensive. How do you reduce memory usage by 5× without losing functionality?
**Answer:** Several techniques combine for big savings: **(1) Use Redis's ziplist / listpack encoding for small structures** — by default, small hashes, lists, and zsets are stored in a compact "ziplist" (now "listpack" in 7.0+) format that uses ~10× less memory than the standard encoding. Tune `hash-max-listpack-entries 512`, `hash-max-listpack-value 64`, `list-max-listpack-size -2`, `zset-max-listpack-entries 128`. This is the single biggest win for many workloads. **(2) Use shorter keys** — `user:42:profile` becomes `u:42:p`. With millions of keys, this saves megabytes. Define a key abbreviation table in your codebase. **(3) Use hashes instead of many string keys** — instead of `SET user:42:name "alice"` + `SET user:42:email "a@x.com"`, use `HSET user:42 name alice email a@x.com` — the hash overhead is amortized. **(4) Compress large values** — for values >1KB, compress with Snappy or Gzip before `SET`. Cache HTML/JSON responses often compress 5-10×. **(5) Set TTLs aggressively** — don't cache anything forever; even a 24-hour TTL lets Redis evict cold data. **(6) Use `maxmemory` + eviction policy** — set `maxmemory 16gb` and `maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru` so Redis evicts least-recently-used keys when full. **(7) Move cold data to disk** — Redis on Flash (commercial) or migrate cold keys to a slower store (DynamoDB, S3). **(8) Use Redis 7.x's listpack** (replaces ziplist, more memory-efficient). **(9) Deduplicate values** — if many keys share the same value, store the value once in a "pool" key and reference it. Real-world: Stack Overflow reduced Redis memory 4× by switching to hashes + listpack; GitHub uses aggressive TTLs and Snappy compression. Combine all techniques and 5× reduction is achievable.
**Visual:**
```
Memory reduction techniques (cumulative):

  Baseline: 1 TB
    + strings stored as standard encoding
    + long keys ("user:42:profile")
    + many small string keys
    + uncompressed JSON values
    + no TTLs (cache forever)
    + no maxmemory limit

  After (1) listpack encoding for small structures:
    1 TB -> 400 GB  (2.5x reduction)
    config: hash-max-listpack-entries 512
            zset-max-listpack-entries 128
            (small hashes/zsets use compact encoding)

  After (2) shorter keys ("u:42:p"):
    400 GB -> 350 GB

  After (3) hashes instead of string keys:
    350 GB -> 200 GB  (amortize overhead)
    before: SET user:42:name ... ; SET user:42:email ...
    after:  HSET user:42 name ... email ...

  After (4) Snappy compression on values >1KB:
    200 GB -> 80 GB  (5x for compressible JSON/HTML)

  After (5) aggressive TTLs (24h max):
    80 GB -> 40 GB  (cold data evicted)

  After (6) maxmemory + LRU eviction:
    40 GB -> 32 GB  (hard cap, evicts LRU)

  Total: 1 TB -> 32 GB (31x reduction)

  Caveats:
    + listpack only for small structures (check config limits)
    + shorter keys = harder to debug (document abbreviations)
    + compression = CPU cost (Snappy is fast, ~1us/KB)
    + TTL = occasional cache miss (acceptable)
    + LRU eviction = some keys evicted early (acceptable for cache)

  For true cold storage:
    + Redis on Flash (commercial, SSD-backed)
    + Migrate cold keys to DynamoDB / S3
    + Use Redis as hot cache + DynamoDB as warm
```
